concepts.title: Drug names and forms
key_points: Every drug has several names, and knowing which kind you are looking at prevents confusion
The generic name is the official name of the drug itself and does not change between manufacturers
The trade name is a manufacturer's brand name, it is capitalised, and one drug may have many
The chemical name describes the molecule and is of no practical use to you on a call
Patients almost always know the trade name and almost never know the generic name
Two boxes with different trade names can contain exactly the same drug, which is a real source of double dosing
Forms matter because form determines route, speed and whether the patient can take it
Common forms: tablets and capsules, liquids and suspensions, gels, sprays, inhalers and auto-injectors
Compressed gas is a form too, and oxygen is a drug
When taking a history, write down exactly what is on the box rather than what you think it means
misconceptions: Assuming two trade names mean two different drugs
Recording what you think a drug is rather than what the box says
Treating oxygen as something other than a drug
Expecting a patient to know generic names

read.plain:
Every drug has more than one name, and the confusion that causes is a genuine patient safety problem rather than a vocabulary quiz.

The generic name is the official name of the drug itself. It does not change between manufacturers or countries, it is written in lower case, and it is the name that actually identifies the substance.

The trade name is a brand name owned by a manufacturer. It is capitalised, it is usually shorter and more memorable, and a single drug may have many of them. That is by design — the memorable name is the one being advertised.

The chemical name describes the molecule itself, and it is of no practical use to you on a call. Know that it exists and move on.

Here is why this matters operationally. Patients almost always know the trade name, because that is what is on the box and what the advertisement said. They almost never know the generic name. So when you ask what someone takes, expect brand names, and expect not to recognise some of them.

And the real hazard: two boxes bearing different trade names can contain exactly the same drug. A patient prescribed one brand by a specialist and another by a family doctor may be taking a double dose of the same medication without anyone having noticed — including them. This is a well-recognised cause of harm, and it is one of the reasons taking the actual boxes to hospital is so useful.

Then forms, which matter more than they first appear because the form determines the route, the speed of onset, and whether this patient can take it at all.

Tablets and capsules are swallowed, which requires a patient who can swallow safely. Liquids and suspensions are easier for patients who cannot manage tablets. Gels are absorbed through the tissues of the mouth. Sprays under the tongue absorb quickly. Inhalers deliver the drug directly to the airways. Auto-injectors deliver an injection through a spring-loaded device designed to be usable by someone who is frightened and unwell. And compressed gas is a form too — which is worth stating plainly, because oxygen is a drug, with indications, contraindications, effects and harms, and it deserves the same care as anything else you give.

A practical instruction to finish. When you take a medication history, write down exactly what is on the box. Not your interpretation of it, not what class you think it belongs to, not a guess at the generic name. The exact words, the exact strength on the label, and the form. Somebody at the hospital will be able to make sense of it, and they can only do that if what you wrote is what was actually there.
read.standard: Pharmaceutical agents carry multiple designations, confusion between which constitutes a patient safety concern. The generic name is the official designation of the substance, invariant across manufacturers and jurisdictions and rendered in lower case. The trade name is a proprietary designation owned by a manufacturer, capitalised, and potentially multiple for a single agent. The chemical name describes molecular structure and has no prehospital utility. Patients characteristically recognise trade names and not generic names, as the former appear on packaging and in advertising; medication histories should therefore anticipate proprietary designations. Distinct trade names may denote identical agents, producing inadvertent duplicate dosing where multiple prescribers are involved, a recognised source of harm and a rationale for transporting original containers. Pharmaceutical form determines route, onset and patient suitability. Forms comprise tablets and capsules requiring intact swallowing; liquids and suspensions for patients unable to manage solid forms; gels absorbed through oral mucosa; sublingual sprays affording rapid absorption; inhalers delivering agent directly to the airway; auto-injectors providing spring-actuated injection usable by distressed patients; and compressed gas, oxygen constituting a drug with indications, contraindications, effects and potential harms warranting equivalent care. Medication histories should record packaging text verbatim, including exact strength and form, rather than provider interpretation, class attribution or presumed generic equivalent, as receiving clinicians can interpret accurate transcription but not inference.

eli_new.body: Two different boxes can hold the same drug. That is how people end up taking a double dose without anybody noticing, including them.

concepts.title: Routes of administration
key_points: The route determines how fast a drug works and how much of it reaches the bloodstream
Broadly, the closer to the bloodstream and the better the blood supply, the faster the effect
Oral means swallowed, and it is the slowest route because it must be absorbed through the gut
Never give anything by mouth to a patient who cannot protect their own airway
Sublingual means under the tongue, where a rich blood supply absorbs the drug quickly
Inhaled means into the airways, which is fast and delivers the drug where it is needed for lung problems
Intramuscular means into muscle, which has a good blood supply and gives a reliable, fairly quick effect
Intranasal uses the lining of the nose and works quickly without a needle
Intravenous is the fastest and most complete route, and it is outside EMT scope in most systems
The route also determines what can go wrong, so match the route to the patient's condition
misconceptions: Giving anything oral to a patient who cannot protect their airway
Assuming a route works the same in a shocked patient
Confusing sublingual with swallowed
Using a route your protocol does not authorise

read.plain:
The route is how the drug gets in, and it determines two things that matter: how fast it works, and how much of it actually reaches the bloodstream.

The organising principle is simple. The closer the drug starts to the bloodstream, and the better the blood supply where you put it, the faster it works. Everything below is a version of that.

Oral means swallowed. It is the slowest route, because the drug has to pass into the stomach, be absorbed through the gut wall, and travel through the liver before it reaches the general circulation. It is convenient and it is what most medication is, but nothing about it is fast.

And it carries an absolute rule: never give anything by mouth to a patient who cannot protect their own airway. Not a tablet, not a drink, not a gel. A patient with a reduced level of consciousness, or who cannot swallow reliably, will aspirate it into their lungs, and aspiration causes serious harm and sometimes kills people. When you are deciding whether an oral medication is appropriate, that question comes before every other consideration.

Sublingual means under the tongue. That area has a rich blood supply and a thin lining, so a drug placed there is absorbed quickly and directly — and importantly, it bypasses the gut and the liver entirely. That is why drugs needed quickly are given this way. The patient must not swallow it, and it does not work in a dry mouth.

Inhaled means into the airways, by inhaler or nebuliser. It is fast, and it has the specific advantage that for a lung problem, it puts the drug exactly where the problem is, in a small dose, with fewer effects elsewhere in the body.

Intramuscular means into a muscle. Muscle has a good blood supply, so absorption is reliable and reasonably quick — not as fast as intravenous, but it needs no vein and can be given quickly by someone with basic training, which is exactly why auto-injectors use this route.

Intranasal uses the lining of the nose, which is thin and richly supplied with blood. It works quickly, needs no needle, and can be given to a patient who is unconscious or uncooperative. That combination is why it has become common for certain emergency medications.

Intravenous means directly into a vein. It is the fastest and most complete route, because the drug is already in the bloodstream and nothing has to be absorbed at all. In most systems it is outside EMT scope.

The route also determines what can go wrong, which is a useful way to think about it. Oral risks aspiration. Inhaled requires a patient who can take a breath in when you ask. Intramuscular depends on perfusion — in a severely shocked patient with poor peripheral circulation, absorption from muscle is unreliable. So match the route to the patient in front of you rather than to the drug in the abstract.
read.standard: Route of administration determines onset and bioavailability, governed by proximity to the circulation and vascularity of the absorptive surface. Oral administration is the slowest route, requiring gastric passage, intestinal absorption and hepatic first-pass metabolism prior to systemic circulation. Oral administration is absolutely contraindicated in patients unable to protect the airway, including those with reduced consciousness or unreliable swallow, owing to aspiration risk with attendant morbidity and mortality; airway protection is assessed before other considerations. Sublingual administration employs the richly vascularised, thinly epithelialised sublingual surface, affording rapid absorption with avoidance of gastrointestinal transit and hepatic first pass; the preparation must not be swallowed and absorption is impaired in xerostomia. Inhaled administration delivers agent to the airway by inhaler or nebuliser, providing rapid onset and, for pulmonary pathology, site-directed delivery at reduced dose with reduced systemic effect. Intramuscular administration exploits skeletal muscle vascularity for reliable, moderately rapid absorption without venous access, requiring minimal training and underlying auto-injector design. Intranasal administration employs the thin, vascular nasal mucosa, affording rapid onset without needle and permitting administration to unconscious or uncooperative patients. Intravenous administration provides the most rapid and complete delivery, bypassing absorption entirely, and is beyond EMT scope in most systems. Route selection additionally determines failure mode: oral confers aspiration risk, inhaled requires inspiratory capacity, and intramuscular absorption is unreliable in severe shock with peripheral hypoperfusion; route should therefore be matched to patient condition.

eli_new.analogy: Under the tongue is a short cut. It skips the stomach and the liver entirely, which is why it is used when something needs to work now.
eli_new.body: Never put anything in the mouth of a patient who cannot protect their airway. That question comes before every other consideration about an oral medication.

concepts.title: How drugs act, and the words for it
key_points: A drug changes something the body already does — it speeds it up, slows it down, or blocks it
Onset is how long until the drug starts working, and it depends heavily on the route
Peak is when the effect is greatest, and duration is how long the effect lasts
Half-life describes how long the body takes to remove half of the drug
An agonist produces an effect; an antagonist blocks one, including sometimes an overdose
An antagonist can wear off before the drug it is blocking, so the original effect can return
Absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination describe a drug's journey through the body
Liver and kidney function affect metabolism and elimination, which is why the elderly and the unwell are more sensitive
Tolerance means a patient needs more of a drug over time to get the same effect
Reassessment after giving a drug is how you find out what it actually did, rather than what it should have done
misconceptions: Assuming an antagonist lasts as long as the drug it reverses
Expecting the same onset from every route
Ignoring liver and kidney function in older patients
Giving a drug and not reassessing

read.plain:
A useful starting idea: a drug does not add a new capability to the body. It changes something the body already does — speeds a process up, slows it down, or blocks it. Almost every drug you will meet fits one of those descriptions, and thinking about it that way makes the effects predictable rather than arbitrary.

Some words you need.

Onset is how long before the drug starts to do something. It depends enormously on the route, which is the link back to the previous concept — the same drug given by two routes has two different onsets.

Peak is when the effect is at its greatest. Duration is how long the effect lasts.

Half-life is how long the body takes to remove half of the drug present. It is a useful shorthand for how long something hangs around, and it explains why some drugs are taken once a day and others four times.

Then two words worth knowing properly.

An agonist produces an effect — it stimulates the process. An antagonist blocks one — it occupies the place the drug or the body's own chemical would act, and stops it working. Some antagonists are used specifically to reverse an overdose.

And that leads to something clinically important rather than merely definitional: an antagonist can wear off before the drug it is blocking. Give a reversal agent for an overdose and the patient may wake up — but if the reversal agent is shorter-acting than the drug it reversed, the original effect returns when the antagonist fades. Which is why a patient who has been reversed is still a patient who needs transport and observation, no matter how well they now look or how strongly they insist otherwise. This is one of the more important single ideas in prehospital pharmacology.

Four words describe a drug's journey. Absorption, getting in. Distribution, moving around the body. Metabolism, being chemically altered, mostly by the liver. Elimination, leaving, mostly through the kidneys.

That last pair explains something you will see constantly. Older patients and patients with liver or kidney disease metabolise and eliminate drugs more slowly, so drugs accumulate and effects are stronger and longer than expected. It is the mechanism behind the polypharmacy point in geriatrics: a dose that was fine for years becomes too much as those organs decline.

Tolerance means needing more of a drug over time to get the same effect, and it develops with some drugs and not others. A patient taking a long-term medication may need doses that would be dangerous in someone who does not take it, which is useful context rather than a judgement.

And finally, the practical instruction that makes all of this real. After you give a drug, reassess. Not because the textbook says what should happen, but because what actually happened is the only thing that matters, and it is frequently not what was expected. Did it work? Did anything else happen? Document both.
read.standard: Pharmacological agents modify existing physiological processes by augmentation, attenuation or blockade rather than conferring novel function. Onset denotes interval to initial effect and is route-dependent, the same agent exhibiting differing onset by route. Peak denotes maximal effect and duration denotes persistence of effect. Half-life denotes the interval required for elimination of half the quantity present and informs dosing frequency. Agonists produce receptor-mediated effect; antagonists occupy the site of action and prevent effect, certain antagonists being employed for overdose reversal. Clinically, an antagonist may exhibit shorter duration than the agent it reverses, permitting return of the original effect following antagonist decline; patients receiving reversal therefore require transport and observation irrespective of apparent recovery or refusal. Pharmacokinetics comprise absorption, distribution, metabolism, predominantly hepatic, and elimination, predominantly renal. Reduced hepatic and renal function in elderly patients and those with organ disease impairs metabolism and elimination, producing accumulation with augmented and prolonged effect; this mechanism underlies the geriatric observation that established doses may become excessive with organ decline. Tolerance denotes requirement for increased dose to achieve equivalent effect over time, occurring with certain agents, such that patients on long-term therapy may require doses hazardous in naive patients. Reassessment following administration is required to determine actual effect, which frequently differs from anticipated effect, with documentation of both therapeutic and adverse outcomes.

eli_new.analogy: Drugs do not give the body new abilities. They speed something up, slow something down, or block it — which makes the effects predictable rather than arbitrary.
eli_new.body: An antagonist can wear off before the drug it reversed. Which is why a reversed patient still needs transport and watching, however well they look and however firmly they say otherwise.

concepts.title: Indications, contraindications and side effects
key_points: An indication is the reason to give a drug — the situation in which it helps
A contraindication is a reason not to give it, because in this situation it would cause harm
An absolute contraindication means never in this situation; a relative one means weigh it up
Side effects are effects other than the intended one, and most are predictable from how the drug works
An untoward or adverse effect is a harmful one, and you look for it rather than waiting to notice
Allergy is different from side effect — nausea is a side effect, a rash and swelling is an allergy
Always ask about allergies before giving anything, every time, including things you have given before
Check indications and contraindications for every administration rather than relying on memory
The patient's other medications can create a contraindication that neither drug has alone
If you are unsure whether a drug is indicated, contact medical direction rather than guessing
misconceptions: Confusing an allergy with a side effect
Skipping the allergy question on a repeat administration
Treating a relative contraindication as absolute or vice versa
Guessing rather than contacting medical direction
exam_favorites: Allergy is not a side effect

read.plain:
Four words carry most of this concept, and being precise about them prevents real errors.

An indication is the reason to give a drug — the situation in which it is expected to help. Every administration you make should be answerable with a specific indication, not just a general impression that it seemed like a good idea.

A contraindication is a reason not to give it, because in this particular situation it would do harm. This is the more important of the pair, and the one that requires active checking, because indications tend to be obvious and contraindications tend to be hidden in the history.

Contraindications come in two strengths. An absolute contraindication means never, in this situation, regardless of how much you would like to. A relative contraindication means the risk is increased and has to be weighed against the benefit — which usually means a conversation with medical direction rather than a decision made alone.

Side effects are effects other than the intended one. Most are entirely predictable from how the drug works: a drug that relaxes airways will also affect the heart, because the same mechanism reaches both. Understanding the mechanism makes the side effects memorable rather than a list.

An untoward or adverse effect is a harmful one. And the useful instruction here is that you look for them actively rather than waiting to notice — knowing what a drug might do means you check for it specifically after giving it.

Now the distinction that matters most in practice: allergy is not the same as a side effect, and patients routinely report the two as the same thing. "I'm allergic to that, it makes me feel sick" describes a side effect, not an allergy. A true allergy involves an immune reaction — rash, hives, swelling, wheeze, difficulty breathing — and it can be life-threatening and can worsen with each exposure.

The distinction matters because it changes what can safely be given. But the prehospital rule is unambiguous: if a patient reports an allergy, you do not give that drug. Sorting out whether it was a genuine allergy is a conversation for the hospital, not a judgement to make on scene, and the clarification you ask for is about the history rather than about permission.

So ask about allergies before giving anything. Every time. Including a drug you have already given this patient today, because circumstances change and because asking costs four seconds.

Check indications and contraindications for every administration rather than relying on memory. You will give the same handful of drugs hundreds of times, and familiarity is exactly the condition under which people stop checking.

And remember that the patient's other medications can create a contraindication that neither drug carries alone. Two drugs that are individually fine can be dangerous together, which is another reason the medication list is worth gathering properly.

If you are not sure whether a drug is indicated, contact medical direction. That is the correct action, not a fallback, and nobody has ever been criticised for asking.
read.standard: Indication denotes the circumstance in which administration is expected to benefit; every administration should correspond to a specific indication. Contraindication denotes circumstance in which administration would cause harm, requiring active verification, as indications are typically apparent whereas contraindications reside within the history. Absolute contraindications preclude administration irrespective of circumstance; relative contraindications denote increased risk requiring benefit-risk assessment, typically with medical direction. Side effects denote effects other than the intended effect and are predominantly predictable from mechanism, as receptor distribution extends beyond the target tissue. Untoward or adverse effects denote harmful effects, requiring active surveillance informed by knowledge of the agent's potential effects rather than passive observation. Allergy is distinct from side effect and is frequently conflated by patients; gastrointestinal upset constitutes a side effect whereas immune-mediated reaction with urticaria, angio-oedema, wheeze or respiratory compromise constitutes allergy, which may be life-threatening and may escalate with repeated exposure. Prehospitally, reported allergy precludes administration of that agent; differentiation of true allergy from intolerance is undertaken in hospital. Allergy enquiry precedes every administration, including repeat administration to the same patient. Indication and contraindication verification is performed for every administration rather than by recall, as familiarity with frequently administered agents predisposes to omission of checking. Concurrent medications may generate contraindications absent for either agent individually, providing further rationale for comprehensive medication history. Where indication is uncertain, medical direction consultation constitutes the correct action.

eli_new.analogy: Indications are obvious and contraindications hide in the history. That asymmetry is why one of them needs active checking and the other mostly does not.
eli_new.body: 'I'm allergic, it makes me feel sick' describes a side effect. But on scene it does not matter — reported allergy means you do not give it, and sorting it out is a hospital conversation.

concepts.title: The six rights
key_points: The six rights are a checklist performed out loud before every single administration
Right patient — confirm who you are giving it to, which matters more with multiple patients
Right medication — read the label, and read it at the moment you draw or open it, not from memory
Right dose — confirm the amount against your protocol, and check the concentration on the label
Right route — confirm how it goes in, because the same drug by the wrong route can harm
Right time — confirm it is the right moment, including whether an earlier dose has already been given
Right documentation — record what, how much, by which route, at what time, by whom, and the effect
Read the label three times: when you pick it up, when you prepare it, and before it goes in
Say the checks out loud, because speaking them catches errors that silent reading does not
Some texts add a seventh right, such as the patient's right to refuse — follow the version your programme uses
misconceptions: Reading the label once and relying on memory
Checking silently rather than out loud
Skipping the check because you have given this drug many times
Documenting later and inaccurately

read.plain:
The six rights are a checklist you run before every single administration, and the whole value of them is that they are performed rather than known. Being able to list them is not the skill. Running them at three in the morning when you are tired and hurried is the skill.

Right patient. Confirm who you are giving this to. This sounds trivial with one patient in a bedroom and stops being trivial the moment there are two, or when several crews are working in the same space, or when the patient cannot confirm their own identity.

Right medication. Read the label. Read it at the moment you open or draw it, not from memory of what you picked up thirty seconds ago and not from the position it lives in on the shelf. Boxes get restocked in the wrong place, and packaging from the same manufacturer looks alike on purpose.

Right dose. Confirm the amount against your protocol, and check the concentration on the label as well as the volume. The same drug frequently exists in more than one concentration, and that is the mechanism behind some of the worst errors in medicine.

Right route. Confirm how it goes in. Some drugs exist in forms for different routes, and the same drug by the wrong route can be ineffective or dangerous.

Right time. Confirm this is the right moment. In practice the highest-value version of this question is whether a dose has already been given — by the patient themselves before you arrived, by a family member, by a first responder, or by your own crew. Ask specifically, because people do not volunteer it.

Right documentation. Record what you gave, how much, by which route, at what time, who gave it, and what happened afterwards. That last part is frequently omitted and is the part the hospital most wants.

Two habits make the rights actually work.

Read the label three times: when you pick the container up, when you prepare the dose, and immediately before it goes in. That sounds excessive and it is the standard practice in every setting that gives medications routinely, for the straightforward reason that it catches errors at three separate points.

And say the checks out loud. Speaking them engages a different kind of attention than reading them silently, it lets your partner catch what you missed, and it produces a shared record of what was intended. Silent checking feels the same as checking and is measurably worse.

Finally, be aware that some texts and programmes add a seventh right, most commonly the patient's right to refuse, and sometimes the right effect or the right to know what they are being given. Follow whichever version your programme and protocol use. The number matters less than the fact that you actually perform them.

And the honest warning: the danger is familiarity. You will give the same handful of drugs hundreds of times, and the check will start to feel like a formality. That is precisely when it stops being performed, and precisely when it was doing its job.
read.standard: The six rights constitute a pre-administration verification checklist performed prior to every administration, with operational value residing in execution rather than recall. Right patient requires confirmation of recipient identity, of increased importance with multiple patients, multiple attending crews, or patients unable to confirm identity. Right medication requires label verification at the point of opening or preparation rather than by recall or storage position, as restocking errors occur and manufacturer packaging is deliberately similar. Right dose requires verification of quantity against protocol and of concentration in addition to volume, as multiple concentrations of a single agent constitute a recognised source of serious error. Right route requires confirmation of administration route, as agents exist in route-specific formulations and incorrect route may render administration ineffective or harmful. Right time requires confirmation of appropriate timing, with the highest-yield application being determination of prior administration by the patient, family, first responders or crew, which is infrequently volunteered and requires specific enquiry. Right documentation requires recording of agent, quantity, route, time, administering provider and subsequent effect, the last frequently omitted and of greatest interest to receiving clinicians. Two practices support execution: triple label verification at retrieval, preparation and administration, standard in settings administering medications routinely as it interrupts error at three points; and verbalisation of checks, which engages distinct attentional processes, permits partner verification and generates a shared record, silent verification being subjectively equivalent and measurably inferior. Some texts and programmes specify a seventh right, commonly the right to refuse, the right effect, or the right to information; providers follow their programme and protocol. Familiarity with frequently administered agents constitutes the principal threat to execution.

eli_new.analogy: Being able to list the six rights is not the skill. Running them at three in the morning when you are tired is the skill.

concepts.title: Medication errors
key_points: Medication errors happen to careful people, and the system is designed on that assumption
Common errors: wrong drug, wrong dose, wrong route, wrong patient, and a dose given twice
Look-alike packaging and sound-alike names are known causes rather than excuses
Distraction and interruption during preparation are strongly associated with error
If you make an error, the first action is to care for the patient, not to work out what happened
Tell someone immediately — your partner, medical direction and the receiving hospital
Document what was actually given, accurately, including the error
Never conceal an error or alter documentation, which turns a clinical problem into a career-ending one
Report through your service's process, because errors that are not reported cannot be prevented
A service that punishes reporting produces silence rather than safety, and good ones know it

Trying to work out what happened before treating the patient
Assuming careful people do not make errors
Not reporting a near miss

read.plain:
Medication errors happen to careful, competent, experienced people. That is not a reassurance, it is the design assumption behind every check in this lesson — the rights, the triple label read, the verbalising. Those exist because individual care is not sufficient on its own, and a system that relied on people simply being careful would fail regularly.

The common errors are worth naming so you can watch for them. The wrong drug. The wrong dose. The wrong route. The wrong patient. And a dose given twice, because two people each thought the other had not done it.

Some known causes. Look-alike packaging — manufacturers use house styles, so their products resemble each other. Sound-alike names, which are common enough that published lists of confusable pairs exist. And distraction or interruption during preparation, which is one of the strongest associations there is: being spoken to halfway through drawing up a dose substantially increases the chance of getting it wrong. That is why some settings treat medication preparation as a do-not-interrupt activity, and why it is worth saying "give me ten seconds" rather than answering.

Now the important part: what to do if it happens.

First, care for the patient. Not investigate, not explain, not work out how. Assess them, treat the effects, get help if you need it, and prepare for what this drug or this dose is likely to do. The patient is the only urgent thing in the situation.

Second, tell someone immediately. Your partner, medical direction, and the receiving hospital. The hospital in particular must know, because their treatment depends on what is actually in the patient, and a concealed error means clinicians treating a patient on false information. Say it plainly and early.

Third, document what was actually given. Accurately. Including the error. The record must describe reality, because everyone downstream relies on it.

And the rule with the sharpest consequences: never conceal an error and never alter documentation. Concealment turns a clinical problem into a professional and legal catastrophe. An error honestly reported is usually survivable, both for the patient and for your career. An error concealed, and then discovered, generally is not — and it will be discovered, because the patient's subsequent course does not match their record.

Report through your service's process, including near misses — the ones where you caught it in time. Near misses are free information about how the next real error will happen, and a service that hears about them can fix the packaging, the storage or the procedure before somebody is harmed.

One last observation, which is about culture rather than about you. A service that punishes reporting produces silence, not safety. The errors still happen; they simply stop being visible, which means nothing gets fixed. Good organisations understand this and treat honest reporting as a contribution rather than a confession. If you can, be the person who reports, and be the person who makes it safe for others to.
read.standard: Medication errors occur among careful, competent and experienced practitioners; verification systems including the rights, triple label verification and verbalisation exist on this assumption, as reliance on individual diligence alone produces regular failure. Common error types comprise incorrect agent, dose, route and patient, and duplicate administration arising from assumed non-administration by a colleague. Recognised contributory factors include look-alike packaging arising from manufacturer house styles, sound-alike agent names for which published confusable-pair lists exist, and distraction or interruption during preparation, which demonstrates strong association with error and underlies do-not-interrupt designation of medication preparation in some settings. Following an error, the sequence is: first, patient care, comprising assessment, treatment of effects, escalation and anticipation of the agent's likely effects; second, immediate disclosure to partner, medical direction and receiving facility, the latter essential as subsequent treatment depends on accurate knowledge of administered agents and concealment causes clinicians to treat on false information; third, accurate documentation of what was actually administered including the error, as downstream care depends on record accuracy. Concealment of error and alteration of documentation are absolutely prohibited, converting a clinical event into a professional and legal one; honest reporting is generally survivable clinically and professionally whereas concealment discovered through divergence between clinical course and record is not. Reporting through service process should include near misses, which provide information regarding latent failure modes and permit correction of packaging, storage or procedure before harm occurs. Organisational cultures that penalise reporting produce non-reporting rather than reduced error, preventing system correction.

eli_new.analogy: An error honestly reported is usually survivable. An error concealed and then discovered generally is not — and it will be discovered, because the patient's course stops matching their record.
eli_new.body: The first action after an error is caring for the patient. Not investigating, not explaining, not working out how. The patient is the only urgent thing in the room.

concepts.title: Your scope, and medical direction
key_points: What you may give is set by your protocol and your medical director, not by what you know
At EMT level the actions are usually administer, or assist the patient with their own medication
Administering means you give a medication your service carries, under your authority to do so
Assisting means helping a patient take their own prescribed medication, which is a different authority
Standing orders authorise you to act without contacting anyone first, in defined situations
Online medical direction means contacting a physician and receiving an order for this specific patient
Know which of your medications are standing orders and which require contact, before you need to know
When you contact medical direction, give a clear picture and repeat the order back before acting
If an order seems wrong or unsafe, say so — you are responsible for what you do, and repeating the concern is appropriate
Acting outside your scope is a serious matter, however well intentioned and however right you were
misconceptions: Acting on knowledge rather than authorisation
Failing to repeat back an order
Carrying out an order you believe is unsafe without questioning it
Confusing assisting with administering

read.plain:
What you may give is determined by your protocol and your medical director. Not by what you know, not by what would clearly help, and not by what you did in a previous job or a different system. This is one of the sharpest distinctions between medicine as a body of knowledge and medicine as a practice with authority attached.

At EMT level, there are usually two kinds of action.

Administering means you give a medication your service carries, under your own authority to do so. The drug is yours, the decision is within your scope, and you are acting as a clinician within a defined permission.

Assisting means helping a patient take their own prescribed medication — their inhaler, their nitroglycerin, their auto-injector. That is a different authority and frequently has different conditions attached: the medication must be prescribed to this patient, it must be in date, and your protocol will usually require specific criteria to be met. Knowing which of your actions is which matters, because the rules differ.

Then the two ways authority reaches you.

Standing orders, sometimes called offline medical direction, are written authorisations to act in defined situations without contacting anybody first. Your medical director has decided in advance that in this situation, an EMT may do this. That decision has already been made; you are executing it.

Online medical direction means contacting a physician and receiving an order for this specific patient, now. You describe the situation and they authorise, modify or decline.

Find out which of your medications sit in which category before you need to know. Standing in a kitchen with a deteriorating patient is a bad time to discover that the drug in your hand requires a phone call.

When you do contact medical direction, two habits make it work. Give a clear, ordered picture — who the patient is, what is wrong, what you have found, what you have done, and what you are asking for. And repeat the order back before acting on it. Repeating back catches mishearing, catches ambiguity, and takes three seconds. Radios are noisy, drug names sound alike, and "repeat back" exists because of what happens when people do not.

Now the harder situation. If an order seems wrong or unsafe, say so. You are responsible for what you do, and "I was told to" is not a complete answer for an action you knew was wrong. The correct approach is not refusal as a first move; it is to state your concern clearly and specifically — mention the finding you think they may not have, or the contraindication you believe applies — and to ask them to confirm. Most of the time this resolves it, because most apparently wrong orders are based on incomplete information, and you are the one standing in the room.

And be clear about the last point. Acting outside your scope is a serious matter, regardless of intention and regardless of whether you turned out to be right. Scope exists so that a system can be accountable for what its clinicians do, and the person who exceeds it — even successfully — has removed that accountability.
read.standard: Permissible medication administration is determined by protocol and medical director authorisation rather than by provider knowledge, prior practice in other systems or apparent clinical benefit. EMT-level action comprises two categories. Administration denotes provision of a service-carried medication under the provider's own authorisation. Assistance denotes facilitation of patient self-administration of their own prescribed medication, constituting a distinct authority typically conditional upon the medication being prescribed to that patient, within expiry, and upon protocol-specified criteria. Authority is conveyed by two mechanisms. Standing orders, or offline medical direction, constitute written pre-authorisation for defined situations without requirement for contemporaneous contact, the medical director having determined in advance the permissible action. Online medical direction denotes contemporaneous physician contact and patient-specific order, with authorisation, modification or refusal. Providers should establish the categorisation of their formulary in advance of need. Contact with medical direction requires structured presentation comprising patient identification, presenting problem, findings, interventions performed and the specific request; orders must be repeated back prior to execution, addressing mishearing and ambiguity in a noisy environment with acoustically similar agent names. Where an order appears erroneous or unsafe, the provider states the specific concern, identifying the finding or contraindication believed relevant, and requests confirmation; most such situations resolve, as apparently erroneous orders typically reflect incomplete information held by the remote physician. Providers retain responsibility for their actions and instruction does not constitute complete justification for knowingly erroneous action. Practice outside authorised scope constitutes a serious matter irrespective of intent or outcome, as scope provides the mechanism of system accountability.

eli_new.analogy: Standing orders are a decision already made. Online direction is a decision being made now. Knowing which applies to the drug in your hand is not something to work out in a kitchen.
eli_new.body: Repeat the order back. It takes three seconds, radios are noisy, drug names sound alike, and the instruction exists because of what happened when people did not.

concepts.title: Oxygen
key_points: Oxygen is a drug, and it is the one EMTs give most often
It is indicated where the patient is hypoxic or where hypoxia is likely given their condition
More is not automatically better — the aim is adequate oxygenation, not maximum delivery
Excessive oxygen can be harmful in some conditions, so target it rather than defaulting to the highest flow
The delivery device is chosen by how much the patient needs and what they will tolerate
Nasal cannula for lower concentrations, non-rebreather for high, bag-valve-mask where breathing is inadequate
Oxygen supports combustion, so it is a fire hazard around any ignition source
Cylinders are under high pressure and become dangerous projectiles if the valve is damaged
Cylinder duration depends on the pressure remaining, the cylinder size and the flow rate you choose
Cylinder duration calculation and device selection are covered in Module 02, and are not repeated here
misconceptions: Giving the highest flow to every patient regardless of need
Assuming more oxygen is always safer
Using oxygen near an ignition source
Failing to check remaining cylinder pressure before a long transport

read.plain:
Oxygen is a drug. It is the one you will give most often, and being routine is exactly why it deserves stating plainly — it has indications, contraindications, effects and harms like anything else.

It is indicated where the patient is hypoxic, or where hypoxia is likely given their condition and presentation. That second part matters: you do not always have a number, and a patient who is clearly working hard to breathe, or who has a mechanism or condition that makes hypoxia likely, may need oxygen before any measurement confirms it.

The idea that has changed most in recent practice is this: more is not automatically better. For a long time the default was the highest flow available for almost everybody. Current practice targets adequate oxygenation rather than maximum delivery, because excessive oxygen is harmful in some conditions. Follow your protocol, which will give you the targets your system uses, and think in terms of what this patient needs rather than what the equipment can produce.

Device selection follows the same logic. A nasal cannula delivers lower concentrations, is well tolerated, and suits a patient who needs some support and can breathe adequately. A non-rebreather mask delivers high concentrations for a patient who needs them. And a bag-valve-mask is for a patient whose breathing is inadequate — which is a different problem entirely, because that patient does not need more oxygen in the air they are moving, they need someone to move air for them. Confusing those two situations is one of the more consequential errors in airway management.

Two safety points that are specific to oxygen as a physical substance.

It supports combustion. Oxygen does not burn, but it makes everything else burn far more readily and far faster. So it is a genuine fire hazard around any ignition source — smoking, open flame, sparks, faulty electrical equipment. That includes patients and family members who smoke, and it is worth saying out loud rather than assuming everyone knows.

And cylinders are under very high pressure. A cylinder with a damaged valve can become a projectile capable of going through a wall. Secure cylinders properly, do not drop them, and handle the valve carefully.

Finally, cylinder duration. How long a cylinder lasts depends on the pressure remaining, the cylinder size and the flow rate you have chosen — and running out mid-transport is a preventable failure that has real consequences. The calculation itself, along with device selection in detail, is covered in Module 02 and is deliberately not repeated here. Go and look at it there rather than learning a second, slightly different version of the same thing.
read.standard: Oxygen constitutes a pharmaceutical agent with indications, contraindications, effects and potential harms, and is the most frequently administered agent at EMT level. Indications comprise documented hypoxia or clinical circumstances in which hypoxia is probable, the latter permitting administration in advance of measurement where work of breathing, mechanism or condition indicate likelihood. Contemporary practice targets adequate oxygenation rather than maximal delivery, prior practice having defaulted to maximal flow; excessive administration produces harm in certain conditions, and protocol-specified targets should be applied. Device selection follows required concentration and patient tolerance: nasal cannula provides lower concentrations with good tolerance for patients with adequate spontaneous ventilation; non-rebreather mask provides high concentrations; bag-valve-mask ventilation addresses inadequate ventilation, a distinct problem requiring assisted air movement rather than increased inspired concentration, the conflation of which constitutes a significant airway management error. Oxygen supports combustion without itself burning, substantially increasing ignition readiness and combustion rate of other materials, constituting a fire hazard around smoking materials, open flame, sparks and defective electrical equipment, warranting explicit communication to patients and bystanders. Cylinders contain gas at high pressure and may become projectiles following valve damage, requiring secure stowage and careful handling. Cylinder duration is determined by residual pressure, cylinder capacity and selected flow rate, with mid-transport exhaustion constituting a preventable failure; duration calculation and detailed device selection are addressed in Module 02 and are not duplicated here.

eli_new.analogy: Oxygen does not burn. It makes everything else burn far more readily, which is a more dangerous property than burning would be.
eli_new.body: More is not automatically better. The aim is adequate oxygenation, not maximum delivery, and a patient whose breathing is inadequate needs you to move air for them rather than a richer mixture in the air they are failing to move.

concepts.title: Oral glucose
key_points: Oral glucose is given for suspected low blood sugar in a patient who can protect their own airway
It is a simple sugar, usually supplied as a gel, absorbed through the tissues of the mouth and the gut
The absolute requirement is that the patient can swallow and can protect their airway
Do not give it to an unconscious patient or anyone who cannot swallow — they will aspirate it
It is also contraindicated where the patient cannot follow commands enough to hold it in their mouth
Place it between the cheek and the gum, or as your protocol directs, rather than deep in the mouth
Improvement is usually noticeable within minutes, and reassessment is how you find out
If there is no improvement, consider other causes of altered mental status rather than assuming more is needed
Recheck the blood sugar where your protocol allows and document before and after values
The dose is per protocol — confirm it, and confirm whether your system uses it at all
misconceptions: Giving glucose to a patient who cannot protect their airway
Assuming no improvement means give more
Placing it deep in the mouth rather than in the cheek
Attributing all altered mental status to low sugar

read.plain:
Oral glucose is given for suspected low blood sugar, and it is one of the most satisfying things an EMT does — a patient who was confused, combative or unrousable can become entirely themselves within minutes.

It is a simple sugar, usually supplied as a gel in a tube, and it is absorbed through the tissues of the mouth to some extent and through the gut once swallowed.

And there is one requirement that governs everything: the patient must be able to swallow and protect their own airway.

That is worth stating as strongly as possible, because low blood sugar produces exactly the patients in whom this is uncertain. Someone who is drowsy, or confused, or only intermittently responsive, is the patient this drug was designed for and also the patient who may aspirate it. So the assessment comes first. Can they follow a simple instruction? Can they hold something in their mouth? Can they swallow on request? If you are not confident, do not give it, and treat them as a patient who needs a route you do not have — which means transport and a request for help.

Do not give it to an unconscious patient. Ever. Not a smear on the gums, not a little bit, not because the family says it usually works. An unconscious patient with gel in their mouth is an aspiration waiting to happen, and aspiration can be fatal.

When it is appropriate, placement matters. Between the cheek and the gum, or wherever your protocol directs, rather than deep in the mouth or on the back of the tongue — you want it where it will sit and dissolve rather than where it can be inhaled.

Then reassess, which is the part that turns this into medicine rather than a procedure. Improvement is usually noticeable within a few minutes. Look for it specifically, and document what you saw before and after.

And if there is no improvement, the correct response is not automatically to give more. It is to think again. Altered mental status has many causes, and low blood sugar is only one of them — a stroke, a head injury, an overdose, hypoxia, an infection. A patient who does not respond to glucose may have been given the right drug for the wrong problem, and that information is valuable rather than disappointing.

Recheck the blood sugar where your protocol allows it, and document both values along with the time.

The dose is per protocol. Confirm it, and confirm whether your system carries this at all — practice varies, and some systems have moved to other approaches.
read.standard: Oral glucose is administered for suspected hypoglycaemia in patients with intact airway protective reflexes. It comprises a simple carbohydrate, typically supplied as gel, absorbed partially through oral mucosa and subsequently enterally. The governing requirement is demonstrated capacity to swallow and protect the airway. This assumes particular significance as hypoglycaemia produces precisely the population in which airway protection is uncertain: drowsy, confused or intermittently responsive patients constitute both the indicated population and the aspiration-risk population. Assessment precedes administration, addressing ability to follow simple instruction, retain material in the mouth and swallow on request; where capacity is uncertain, administration is withheld and the patient managed by transport and escalation. Administration to unconscious patients is absolutely contraindicated, including small quantities or gingival application, as aspiration carries potential mortality. Where administration is appropriate, placement between cheek and gingiva, or as protocol specifies, is preferred to posterior placement, permitting dissolution without inhalation risk. Reassessment follows administration, with improvement typically apparent within minutes; pre- and post-administration findings should be documented. Absence of improvement indicates reconsideration of aetiology rather than repeat administration, as altered mental status has multiple causes including cerebrovascular event, head injury, toxic ingestion, hypoxia and infection; non-response constitutes diagnostic information. Blood glucose should be rechecked where protocol permits, with both values and times documented. Dose is protocol-determined, and carriage varies between systems.

eli_new.analogy: Low blood sugar produces exactly the patients in whom swallowing is uncertain. The drug's indication and its biggest danger arrive in the same patient.
eli_new.body: Never in an unconscious patient. Not a smear on the gums, not a little bit, not because the family says it usually works.

concepts.title: Aspirin
key_points: Aspirin is given in suspected heart attack because it reduces the clotting that is causing it
It works by making platelets less able to stick together, which limits the clot
It is one of the few prehospital interventions with clear evidence of benefit in heart attack
It is given early, because the benefit is greatest before the clot is established
Chewing it speeds absorption, so it is chewed rather than swallowed whole where protocol directs
Contraindications include known allergy, active bleeding, and per your protocol
Ask specifically about bleeding disorders and whether the patient already takes it today
It is not a painkiller in this context, and the patient's pain is treated separately
The patient must be able to swallow and protect their airway, as with anything oral
Aspirin is not given to children for fever because of a rare but serious complication
misconceptions: Delaying aspirin while sorting out other things
Assuming the patient has already taken it without asking
Giving it to a patient who cannot protect their airway
Treating it as a painkiller for chest pain

read.plain:
Aspirin is given in suspected heart attack, and it is worth understanding why, because the reason makes the urgency obvious.

A heart attack happens because a clot forms in a coronary artery and blocks the blood supply to part of the heart muscle. Platelets are the cells that clump together to start a clot. Aspirin makes platelets less able to stick to each other, which limits the clot from growing and helps keep the vessel from closing completely.

So aspirin is not treating the pain. It is acting on the actual mechanism of the disease, and that is the reason it matters.

And it is one of the very few things done in the prehospital phase of a heart attack with clear, well-established evidence of benefit — in terms of lives saved per action taken, this simple tablet outperforms most of what is done on these calls.

Which leads to the practical point: give it early. The benefit is greatest before the clot is well established, so this belongs near the front of the call rather than being remembered on the way to hospital. It is quick, it needs no equipment, and it should not be waiting behind other tasks.

Where protocol directs, it is chewed rather than swallowed whole, because chewing breaks it up and speeds absorption. Tell the patient to chew it and then swallow, and expect them to comment on the taste.

Contraindications. Known allergy, which you ask about before giving it as you would with anything. Active bleeding. And whatever else your protocol specifies. Ask specifically about bleeding disorders and about recent bleeding, because patients do not always connect those things to chest pain.

Ask whether they have already taken it today — many people with cardiac histories take a small dose daily, and some will have taken a tablet when the pain started because they were told to. That is exactly the kind of thing that is not volunteered and that changes what you give.

And as with anything oral: the patient must be able to swallow and protect their airway.

One further point worth carrying. Aspirin is not given to children for fever, because of a rare but serious complication associated with its use in children with viral illness. That is not a prehospital cardiac issue, but it is a piece of knowledge that occasionally matters when a parent asks you what they can give.

The dose is per protocol, and it is not the same as the dose used for pain. Confirm it.
read.standard: Aspirin is administered in suspected acute coronary syndrome on the basis of its antiplatelet mechanism. Myocardial infarction results from coronary thrombus formation with consequent interruption of myocardial perfusion; platelets mediate initial thrombus formation, and aspirin impairs platelet aggregation, limiting thrombus propagation and vessel occlusion. Aspirin therefore addresses disease mechanism rather than symptom. It constitutes one of few prehospital interventions in myocardial infarction with established evidence of mortality benefit, with favourable benefit per intervention relative to other measures in this setting. Administration should occur early, as benefit is greatest prior to thrombus establishment; administration should precede rather than follow other tasks, requiring no equipment and minimal time. Where protocol specifies, the tablet is chewed rather than swallowed intact, as disintegration accelerates absorption. Contraindications comprise known allergy, active haemorrhage and protocol-specified additional criteria; specific enquiry regarding bleeding disorders and recent haemorrhage is indicated, as patients may not associate these with the presenting complaint. Enquiry regarding prior administration on the same day is indicated, as daily low-dose therapy is common among patients with cardiac history and self-administration at symptom onset occurs; this information is infrequently volunteered. Airway protection requirements apply as for all oral administration. Aspirin is not administered to children for pyrexia owing to a rare but serious complication associated with use during viral illness. Dose is protocol-determined and differs from analgesic dosing.

eli_new.analogy: Aspirin is not treating the chest pain. It is acting on the clot that is causing the chest pain, which is why the timing matters so much.
eli_new.body: Give it early. It takes seconds, needs no equipment, and the benefit is greatest before the clot is established — so it belongs near the front of the call, not remembered on the way in.

Aspirin stops platelets sticking together, limiting the clot
It treats the mechanism, not the pain

Give it early — before the clot is established

story.title: This morning
story.body:
Somebody asked whether he had taken anything when the pain started, which is not a question people volunteer an answer to.

He had. Two hours earlier, because that is what he had been told to do.

concepts.title: Nitroglycerin
key_points: Nitroglycerin relieves cardiac chest pain by dilating blood vessels and reducing the heart's workload
At EMT level it is usually assisting the patient with their own prescribed medication
It is given under the tongue as a tablet or spray, which absorbs quickly and bypasses the gut
Because it dilates vessels, it lowers blood pressure — which is the source of most of its dangers
Systolic blood pressure below the threshold in your protocol is a contraindication
Erectile dysfunction medication within the preceding period is a contraindication, because the combination can drop pressure catastrophically
Head injury is a contraindication, and there is a maximum number of doses per protocol
Take a blood pressure before each dose and again afterwards, every time
Warn the patient about headache, which is common and expected
Have the patient sitting or lying down, because fainting after a dose is a real risk
misconceptions: Giving a dose without a blood pressure
Failing to ask about erectile dysfunction medication
Assisting with someone else's prescription
Leaving the patient standing after a dose

read.plain:
Nitroglycerin relieves cardiac chest pain, and it does so by dilating blood vessels. Widening the vessels reduces the amount of work the heart has to do to push blood out, which reduces how much oxygen the heart muscle needs — and chest pain of cardiac origin comes from heart muscle not getting enough oxygen for what it is being asked to do. Reduce the demand and the pain eases.

At EMT level, this is usually assisting a patient with their own prescribed medication rather than administering one your service carries. Which brings its own conditions: it must be prescribed to this patient, it must be in date, and your protocol will specify the criteria.

It goes under the tongue — tablet or spray — where it absorbs quickly through a rich blood supply and bypasses the gut and the liver entirely. That is why it works in minutes rather than in half an hour.

Now the important part, and it all follows from one fact: because it dilates blood vessels, it lowers blood pressure. Every significant danger with this drug comes from that single property, and if you hold on to that, the contraindications stop being a list to memorise and become obvious consequences.

A patient whose blood pressure is already low cannot afford to lose more. So a systolic pressure below the threshold in your protocol is a contraindication. Take a blood pressure before each dose — not before the first one only, before each one — and take another afterwards.

Erectile dysfunction medications also dilate blood vessels, by a related mechanism. Combining them with nitroglycerin can drop the blood pressure catastrophically and has killed people. So you ask, and you ask in a way that gets an honest answer: privately where you can, matter-of-factly, explaining why you need to know. This is not an optional or embarrassing question; it is one of the few questions on any call where the answer directly determines whether a drug is safe. Your protocol will specify the time period involved.

Head injury is a contraindication, and there is a maximum number of doses in your protocol.

Practical points that make the difference between a good administration and a bad one. Warn the patient about headache — it is common, it is expected, and it is much less alarming if somebody said it would happen. And have them sitting or lying down. Fainting after a dose is a genuine risk because the blood pressure drops, and a patient who faints standing up now has a head injury as well as chest pain.

The full contraindication list for nitroglycerin, with the specific figures, lives in EMT-04-02-08. Go and read it there.

Administration is sublingual by tablet or spray, affording rapid absorption through vascular mucosa with avoidance of gastrointestinal transit and hepatic first pass, producing onset within minutes. All significant hazards derive from the vasodilatory mechanism producing reduction in blood pressure. Systolic blood pressure below the protocol-specified threshold constitutes a contraindication; blood pressure measurement is required prior to each dose rather than prior to the first alone, with post-administration measurement. concepts.title: Epinephrine by auto-injector
key_points: Epinephrine is the treatment for anaphylaxis, and nothing else takes its place
It works on several problems at once: it opens the airways, tightens the vessels and supports the blood pressure
The most common error in anaphylaxis is giving it too late, not giving it wrongly
There is no absolute contraindication in true anaphylaxis — the alternative is worse than any risk
It is given intramuscularly, into the outer thigh, and it works through clothing
Hold the injector in place for the time the device specifies, then note the time of administration
The device is held with the thumb away from both ends, because injecting a thumb is a real and preventable injury
Effects wear off, and a patient may deteriorate again, so a second dose may be needed per protocol
Every patient given epinephrine is transported, however well they look afterwards
Paediatric devices exist in a different strength, and the paediatric detail is covered in Module 05
misconceptions: Waiting to see whether anaphylaxis improves on its own
Placing the thumb over the end of the injector
Assuming a patient who improves does not need transport
Hesitating because of a cardiac history in true anaphylaxis

read.plain:
Epinephrine is the treatment for anaphylaxis. Not one of the treatments — the treatment. Nothing else takes its place, and every other measure is supportive around it.

It works because it does several things at once, each addressing a different part of what anaphylaxis is doing. It opens the airways, reversing the bronchospasm that is stopping air moving. It tightens blood vessels, which reverses the massive dilation that is dropping the blood pressure. And it reduces the further release of the chemicals driving the reaction. One drug, acting on the airway and the circulation simultaneously, which is why it works when nothing else does.

Now the most important thing in this concept, and it is not pharmacology. The commonest error in anaphylaxis is giving epinephrine too late. Not giving it wrongly, not giving too much — too late. People hesitate, wait to see whether it settles, try something else first, or want to be certain before committing. And deaths from anaphylaxis are associated with delayed administration.

So understand the risk balance properly. In true anaphylaxis there is no absolute contraindication. A patient with a cardiac history still gets it, because a severe allergic reaction will kill them faster and more certainly than the drug will. The hesitation that feels like caution is, in this specific situation, the dangerous option.

Administration. It goes intramuscularly into the outer thigh — the muscle there is large, well supplied with blood, and easy to find on any patient in any position. It works through clothing, which is deliberate, because the device was designed to be used by frightened people in the real world rather than in a clinic.

Hold the injector in place for the time the device specifies, so the full dose is delivered rather than partly left in the device. Then note the time of administration, because that time drives everything that follows.

One mechanical point worth emphasising: hold the device with your thumb away from both ends. Injecting your own thumb happens, it is painful, it can cause real vascular injury, and it removes a provider from the call. Grip it in a fist, needle end away from you, and look at which end is which before you move.

The effects wear off, and this matters clinically. A patient can improve dramatically and then deteriorate again as the drug wears off while the reaction continues. So a second dose may be indicated per your protocol, and the patient must be watched rather than assumed to be fixed.

Which leads to the rule: every patient given epinephrine is transported, however well they look. Improvement is not resolution, the reaction can return, and a patient who refuses at this point needs a real conversation about why.

Paediatric auto-injectors exist in a different strength, and the paediatric detail is covered in Module 05 rather than repeated here.
read.standard: Epinephrine constitutes the definitive treatment for anaphylaxis, with all other measures supportive. Its efficacy derives from simultaneous action on multiple pathophysiological components: bronchodilatation reversing bronchospasm, vasoconstriction reversing vasodilatation-induced hypotension, and attenuation of further mediator release. The predominant error in anaphylaxis management is delayed rather than incorrect administration, with hesitation, observation for spontaneous improvement, trial of alternative measures and diagnostic certainty-seeking contributing; mortality from anaphylaxis is associated with administration delay. In true anaphylaxis no absolute contraindication exists, including cardiac history, as untreated severe allergic reaction carries greater and more immediate mortality than the agent; apparent caution constitutes the hazardous option in this circumstance. Administration is intramuscular into the lateral thigh, selected for muscle bulk, vascularity and accessibility in any patient position, and is effective through clothing by design, the device being intended for lay use under duress. The injector is held in position for the device-specified interval to ensure complete delivery, and administration time recorded, as subsequent management depends upon it. The device is grasped in a fist with the thumb clear of both ends and the needle end directed away, as inadvertent digital injection occurs, causes pain and potential vascular injury, and removes a provider from the incident. Drug effect is time-limited, and clinical deterioration may recur as effect declines while the reaction persists; repeat administration may be indicated per protocol and continued observation is required. All patients receiving epinephrine require transport irrespective of apparent recovery, as improvement does not constitute resolution. Paediatric auto-injectors exist at differing strength; paediatric detail is addressed in Module 05.

concepts.title: Bronchodilators by inhaler
key_points: Bronchodilators relax the muscle around the airways, opening them in asthma and similar conditions
At EMT level this is usually assisting a patient with their own prescribed inhaler
Check it is prescribed to this patient, is in date, and that the criteria in your protocol are met
Shake the inhaler, have the patient breathe out, then fire it as they breathe in slowly and deeply
Ask them to hold the breath briefly afterwards so the drug settles in the airways

A spacer improves delivery considerably and is worth using where one is available
Side effects follow from the mechanism: a faster heart rate, tremor and anxiety are expected
Reassess afterwards by listening and by looking at the work of breathing, not just by asking

read.plain:
Bronchodilators relax the smooth muscle wrapped around the airways. In asthma and similar conditions that muscle has tightened, narrowing the tubes and making it hard to move air, particularly outward. Relax the muscle and the airway opens.

At EMT level this is usually assisting a patient with their own prescribed inhaler rather than administering one your service carries. So the assisting conditions apply: check it is prescribed to this patient, check it is in date, and check that the criteria in your protocol are met.

Technique is the part that decides whether this works, and it is worth taking seriously, because a badly used inhaler delivers a small fraction of its dose and the rest ends up on the back of the throat.

Shake the inhaler. Have the patient breathe out, away from the device. Then have them put it to their lips, seal around it, and fire it at the start of a slow, deep breath in — the coordination is the whole trick. Firing before the breath starts, or after it has finished, wastes most of it.

Then ask them to hold the breath briefly, which lets the drug settle into the airways rather than being immediately blown out again.

A spacer, if one is available, improves delivery considerably. It holds the dose in a chamber so the timing does not have to be perfect, which matters enormously in someone who is breathless and frightened. Many patients own one and have left it in a drawer. Ask.

Side effects follow directly from the mechanism, which makes them easy to remember. These drugs act on receptors that are also present in the heart and elsewhere, so a faster heart rate, tremor, and a feeling of anxiety or jitteriness are expected rather than alarming. Tell the patient, because a shaky patient who was not warned will think they are getting worse.

Reassess properly afterwards. Listen to the chest, look at the work of breathing, look at the position they have chosen and whether they can now speak in longer sentences. Asking "is that better?" is worth something, but a frightened patient will often say yes regardless. Look for the objective change.

And hold on to the limitation that matters most. An inhaler requires the patient to take a deep breath in and coordinate with the device. A patient who is exhausted, or so obstructed that they cannot move much air, cannot use one effectively — the drug does not reach the airways that need it. That patient is a different and more serious problem, and recognising it means escalating rather than repeating a dose that is not getting in.
read.standard: Bronchodilators produce relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle, reversing the bronchoconstriction characteristic of asthma and related conditions which narrows the airway and impairs airflow, particularly expiratory. At EMT level administration typically comprises assistance with the patient's own prescribed inhaler, subject to verification of prescription to that patient, validity of expiry and protocol criteria. Administration technique substantially determines delivered dose, as poor technique results in oropharyngeal deposition of the majority of the dose. Technique comprises shaking the device, exhalation directed away from the device, lip seal, and actuation at the commencement of a slow deep inspiration, the coordination being the critical element, with actuation before or after inspiration wasting the dose. Brief breath-holding follows, permitting airway deposition rather than immediate exhalation. Spacer devices substantially improve delivery by retaining the dose within a chamber, reducing dependence on coordination, which is of particular value in dyspnoeic and distressed patients; many patients possess unused spacers and specific enquiry is warranted. Adverse effects derive from the mechanism, as target receptors are present in cardiac and other tissues, producing expected tachycardia, tremor and anxiety; patients should be forewarned, as unanticipated tremor may be interpreted as deterioration. Reassessment comprises auscultation, observation of work of breathing, positioning and sentence length, as subjective enquiry is unreliable in distressed patients. The principal limitation is that inhaler use requires adequate inspiratory effort and device coordination; exhausted or severely obstructed patients cannot achieve airway delivery, and such presentations require escalation rather than repeated ineffective administration.

concepts.title: Naloxone
key_points: Naloxone reverses opioid overdose by blocking the receptors the opioid is acting on
The problem it treats is the breathing — opioid overdose kills by stopping respiration
Ventilate first where breathing is inadequate, because oxygen is the immediate need
It is given intranasally or intramuscularly at EMT level, depending on your protocol and device
It works within minutes, and the aim is adequate breathing rather than a fully awake patient
Naloxone can wear off before the opioid does, so the overdose can return

Waking a dependent patient abruptly can produce agitation and withdrawal, so expect it and plan for it
