read.plain:
Naloxone reverses opioid overdose. It works as an antagonist — it occupies the receptors the opioid is acting on and blocks it, which reverses the effect.

But start with what the problem actually is, because it determines what you do first. Opioid overdose kills by stopping breathing. The patient is not dying of being unconscious; they are dying of not breathing. Which means that in a patient whose breathing is inadequate, ventilation comes first. Get oxygen moving, then give the drug. A patient who has been ventilated for two minutes before naloxone is in a far better position than one who received naloxone two minutes earlier while not breathing.

At EMT level naloxone is given intranasally or intramuscularly depending on your protocol and the device your service carries. Both work; neither requires a vein.

It works within minutes. And here is the aim, which is frequently misunderstood: you are aiming for adequate breathing, not for a fully awake patient. A patient who is breathing well but still drowsy is a success. Pushing on until they sit up is not a better outcome, and it makes the next part considerably worse.

Now the thing that matters most, and it comes straight from the pharmacology concept. Naloxone can wear off before the opioid does. Many opioids last considerably longer than the reversal agent, so the patient can wake up, feel fine, want to go home — and then stop breathing again an hour later when the naloxone fades and the opioid is still there.

Which makes the rule absolute: every patient given naloxone needs transport and observation. However well they look. However firmly they insist. However embarrassed they are. This is a conversation worth having properly, and the explanation — that what woke you up will wear off before what put you down — is one most patients actually understand when it is put plainly rather than as an instruction.

Expect the waking to be difficult. In a patient who is opioid dependent, abrupt reversal produces immediate withdrawal: nausea, vomiting, pain, sweating, agitation, and sometimes real aggression. That is not bad behaviour, it is a drug effect, and knowing it is coming lets you handle it well. Be positioned so you are not directly over them. Have the suction ready for the vomiting. Speak calmly, explain what has happened and where they are, and do not crowd them. Waking up surrounded by strangers with no memory of how you got there is frightening before any withdrawal is added.

And finally: naloxone does nothing to a non-opioid cause. If there is no response, the answer is not necessarily more — it is to reconsider the diagnosis. A head injury, low blood sugar, a stroke or a different poisoning all produce unresponsive patients, and a lack of response to naloxone is useful information about which of those you might be dealing with.
read.standard: Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity by competitive antagonism at opioid receptors. Opioid overdose produces mortality through respiratory depression; the patient's critical deficit is ventilation rather than consciousness. Where ventilation is inadequate, assisted ventilation precedes pharmacological reversal, as oxygenation constitutes the immediate requirement and prior ventilation improves outcome relative to reversal administered during apnoea. At EMT level administration is intranasal or intramuscular according to protocol and available device, neither requiring venous access. Onset occurs within minutes. The therapeutic target is adequate ventilation rather than full arousal; a patient ventilating adequately while remaining drowsy represents therapeutic success, and titration to full consciousness confers no benefit while worsening subsequent management. Naloxone duration may be shorter than that of the ingested opioid, permitting recurrence of respiratory depression following naloxone decline while opioid effect persists. Consequently all patients receiving naloxone require transport and observation irrespective of apparent recovery or refusal; explanation that the reversal agent will wear off before the opioid is generally comprehensible to patients when stated plainly. Abrupt reversal in opioid-dependent patients precipitates acute withdrawal comprising nausea, vomiting, pain, diaphoresis, agitation and occasionally aggression; this constitutes a pharmacological effect rather than behavioural issue, and anticipation permits appropriate management including provider positioning outside the patient's immediate reach, suction readiness, calm orientation of the patient to circumstances and location, and avoidance of crowding. Naloxone has no effect on non-opioid aetiologies; absence of response indicates diagnostic reconsideration including head injury, hypoglycaemia, cerebrovascular event and alternative poisoning rather than repeat administration.

read.plain:
Activated charcoal binds certain swallowed poisons inside the gut, so that less of the poison is absorbed into the bloodstream. The charcoal is not absorbed itself; it passes through carrying whatever it has bound.

Three things limit it, and they are the reason practice has changed.

First, it only works on substances it binds, and it does not bind everything. Some important poisons are unaffected by it entirely.

Second, it is time-critical. Its benefit comes from binding poison before it is absorbed, so the value falls away as time passes and absorption proceeds.

Third — and this is the practical one — many systems no longer carry it, and many that do require contact with medical direction before it is used. Practice has moved considerably on this over the years. So find out what your own service does, because assuming is how you end up looking for something that is not on the vehicle.

Now the safety rules, which are absolute.

The patient must be alert enough to swallow and protect their own airway. That is the same rule as every other oral medication, and here it carries extra weight, because aspirated charcoal causes severe lung injury. It is not an inert powder in the lungs; it produces serious and sometimes lasting damage. So an altered mental status, drowsiness, or any doubt about swallowing means no.

And this is exactly the population where doubt is common. Poisoned patients frequently have fluctuating mental status, and a patient who is alert now may not be in ten minutes as the poison takes effect. That trajectory is worth thinking about before you give something that must be swallowed.

It is contraindicated after swallowing a corrosive substance — a strong acid or alkali — for two reasons: it does not help, and it obscures the view for the doctor who will need to look at the damaged tissue. And it is contraindicated after petroleum products, because vomiting them back up carries a high risk of aspiration and lung injury.

Practically: it is genuinely unpleasant to drink. It is black, gritty and unappealing. Explain that honestly rather than pretending otherwise, because a patient who was told it tastes fine and then tastes it will not take the rest. Some patients simply refuse, and that is their right.

And contact medical direction and poison control as your protocol directs. Poisoning is an area where specialist advice is immediately available by telephone and changes management more often than in almost any other presentation. Use it rather than deciding alone.
read.standard: Activated charcoal adsorbs certain ingested toxins within the gastrointestinal tract, reducing systemic absorption; the charcoal itself is not absorbed and transits carrying bound substance. Three factors limit utility. Efficacy is confined to substances it adsorbs, with certain clinically significant toxins unaffected. Benefit is time-dependent, deriving from adsorption prior to absorption and declining with elapsed time. Practice has changed substantially, with many systems no longer carrying the agent and many requiring medical direction authorisation; providers should establish their own service's position. Safety requirements are absolute. The patient must possess sufficient alertness to swallow and protect the airway, the standard oral administration requirement carrying additional weight as charcoal aspiration produces severe and potentially lasting pulmonary injury rather than inert deposition. Altered mental status, drowsiness or uncertainty regarding swallow precludes administration. Poisoned patients characteristically demonstrate fluctuating mental status, and a currently alert patient may deteriorate as absorption proceeds; anticipated trajectory should inform the decision to administer an agent requiring swallowing. Administration is contraindicated following ingestion of corrosive substances, strong acid or alkali, as it confers no benefit and obscures endoscopic visualisation of injured tissue, and following petroleum distillate ingestion owing to aspiration risk on emesis with consequent pulmonary injury. The preparation is organoleptically unpleasant, being black and gritty; honest explanation is preferable, as misrepresentation compromises completion of the dose, and refusal is within patient rights. Medical direction and poison control consultation should occur as protocol directs, specialist telephone advice being immediately available and frequently altering management in toxicological presentations.

story.title: In ten minutes
story.dispatch: Medic 2 — overdose, patient currently alert and cooperative.
story.body:
She was alert enough to drink it, right then, at that moment.

Somebody asked what she was likely to be in ten minutes, given what she had taken and when.

That question is the one worth asking before you give anything that has to be swallowed.

indications: Certain ingested poisons, per protocol and usually with medical direction or poison control advice
contraindications: ALTERED MENTAL STATUS or inability to swallow and protect the airway — ASPIRATED CHARCOAL CAUSES SEVERE LUNG INJURY
CORROSIVE ingestion — strong acid or alkali: no benefit, and it obscures the view of the damaged tissue
PETROLEUM PRODUCTS — high aspiration risk on vomiting
Known allergy
drug.route: Oral — the patient must drink it, and it is black, gritty and genuinely unpleasant. Explain that honestly
drug.onset: TIME-CRITICAL — the benefit falls away as the poison is absorbed
